analysis.one_liner: Caps credit card interest rates at 10% through the end of 2030.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced February 4, 2025 by Bernie Sanders with Republican Josh Hawley, has sat in the Senate Banking Committee with no hearing, markup, or vote since its referral.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill writes a hard cap into federal law: a credit card's annual percentage rate, including finance charges, could not exceed 10%, and fees could not be used to dodge the cap. Lenders that knowingly charge more would forfeit all interest on the debt, and cardholders could sue to get back every interest charge, finance charge, or fee they overpaid within two years. Consumer agencies would enforce violations under the Truth in Lending Act. The cap is temporary — it expires January 1, 2031.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly 45% of American households that carry a credit card balance month to month, who currently pay average rates above 20% and as much as 30% or more. A household carrying a few thousand dollars in revolving debt would save hundreds of dollars a year in interest. Cardholders who were overcharged would gain a private right to recover the full amount, not just statutory damages.

how_it_helps.text: Caps the credit card APR, inclusive of all finance charges, at 10 percentage points, down from average rates that have exceeded 20%, with the cap running until January 1, 2031.
Prevents evasion through fees: fees that are not counted as finance charges cannot be used to get around the cap, and their total cannot exceed the total finance charges on the account.

Makes knowing violations cost the lender its entire interest on the debt, and gives cardholders two years to sue and recover the full amount of interest, finance charges, or fees they paid over the cap.

Leaves stronger state-level caps in place by explicitly not preempting state laws that give consumers more protection, and subjects violations to Truth in Lending Act civil liability enforced by the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau and the Federal Trade Commission.

analysis.who_pays: Credit card issuers — the large banks and card companies whose interest income on revolving balances is a major profit center. They would collect far less interest on the roughly half of accounts that carry balances. Some higher-risk borrowers could face reduced access to new credit if issuers tighten underwriting or shift costs to annual fees.

drawbacks.text: A hard 10% cap means issuers cannot price risk: borrowers with poor or thin credit histories, who today pay high rates for access to credit, could be denied cards entirely or offered much smaller limits, since lenders cannot charge enough to cover their default risk.

Issuers could offset lost interest revenue by raising annual fees, cutting cash-back and rewards programs, or tightening credit lines, which would shift some of the cost to cardholders who pay in full — although the bill limits how far fees can go by capping total non-finance-charge fees at the level of finance charges.
The cap is temporary: it sunsets on January 1, 2031, so the relief would lapse unless Congress extends it, and it is set to begin only after enactment rather than being phased in.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the millions of households already carrying balances at 20%–30% rates, a 10% cap is a direct, large saving, and the bill is built to be hard to game: fees are capped relative to finance charges, violators forfeit all interest, and cardholders can claw back overcharges in court. The real cost falls on a small group of higher-risk borrowers whose access to revolving credit could shrink, and on rewards-earning customers if issuers cut benefits. Economists disagree about the size of that access loss; comparable state caps have coexisted with functioning credit markets. The sunset in 2031 limits both the help and the harm.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Banking Committee on the day it was introduced, and the committee has taken no further action on it.

narrative.text: Bernie Sanders introduced the bill on February 4, 2025 'for himself and Mr. Hawley,' pairing the Independent senator with a conservative Republican in an unusual left-right coalition.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs.
Three senators had signed on as cosponsors — two Democrats and one Republican — by the record's latest listing.
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action has followed the referral, leaving the bill pending with no path to a vote so far.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, credit card issuers — they keep collecting interest above 20% while the bill sits without committee action. Nobody has voted on it, so no member is on record either way.

for.name: Bernie Sanders
for.what_they_did: Introduced the 10 Percent Credit Card Interest Rate Cap Act and recruited bipartisan cosponsorship.

for.name: Josh Hawley
for.what_they_did: Joined Sanders as the bill's co-lead, putting a conservative Republican behind a hard cap on card interest.

for.name: Donald Trump
for.what_they_did: Publicly called for capping credit card interest rates at around 10%, lending presidential-level attention to the idea this bill enacts.

against.name: Tim Scott
against.role: Chair, Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee the bill was referred to, has not scheduled a hearing or markup on it; the bill has sat without action since its February 2025 referral.

against.name: Credit card issuers and banking trade groups
against.role: Card-issuing banks and their industry associations
against.what_they_did: Oppose hard interest rate caps, arguing they would restrict credit access and raise fees; the industry has long lobbied against federal rate caps.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's sponsorship is bipartisan from the start — an Independent and a Republican lead it, with three cosponsors split 2 Democrats and 1 Republican — but no chamber has voted on it, so there is no roll-call record of where the parties stand.

industries.note: Interest on revolving balances is one of the most profitable lines in consumer banking; a 10% cap inclusive of finance charges would cut deeply into that revenue. The industry has consistently opposed federal rate caps, which would leave cardholders paying rates several times higher than the proposed ceiling.

Issuers cannot price default risk above 10% under the cap, so some high-risk borrowers could lose access to revolving credit altogether — a real cost — while borrowers who do get cards pay far less. The bill's fee limits would also constrain lenders' room to recover costs through annual fees.

analysis.trajectory: With three cosponsors, no Banking Committee action six months after referral, and a committee chair who has not moved it, the bill is very unlikely to get a hearing or vote this Congress unless the White House makes the 10% cap a legislative priority. Its prior-congressional predecessors died the same way. The Sanders-Hawley pairing keeps it alive as a talking point more than as moving legislation.
